Land Grabs

By: Sophia Phirippides | Production

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

Unique Selling Point:
In the past few days illegal land occupation took an escalating turn. This follows the ANC and the EFF’s radical stance in parliament on Land expropriation without compensation. Raising tensions and misinformation has fueled aggravated individuals on the ground putting people’s homes and safety on the line as private property is invaded.

Summary:
This past weekend Pretoria was marred by illegal land invasion as incidents in Olievenhoutbosch, East Lynne and the Blue hills caught the headlines. Land grabs in South Africa, particularly in Pretoria, were encouraged about two years ago led by the comments made at the time by EFF leader Julius Malema when he said that people must occupy land where they see it. In Mahube, Mamelodi residents were up in arms after EFF supports erected shacks next to their homes following their leader’s message in 2016. Although Land grabbing is not a new thing in South Africa, it is a strange coincidence that this passed weekend’s incidents come just 2 weeks after parliament’s promise to the masses that the “Land is coming”.

On Saturday 10th of March, the Tshwane metro police were forced to use rubber bullets on land invaders. According to Freddie Pienaar, DA ward councilor in East Lynne, the squatters begin erecting shacks along Jan Coetzee and Lanham roads. Freddie believes this was a move that had been planned for sometime although he cannot confirm the instigators. He had to call the Police and Land invasion authorities to come rescue the situation. At the same time in Mnandi, Olievenhoutbosch, residents were also shocked to see people in their privately owned properties marking spaces with poles and saying it now their land. An initiative led by a certain Peter Sealelo, a community leader in Olievenhoutbosch, members of the community have went out to camp on privately owned land claiming that it is unused land that they are now claiming for themselves. A similar case of land grabbing occurred in Blue Hills.


Further information:
Residents in Olievenhoutbosch were threatened and some had to vacate their homes. Rick, one of the resident, says he and his family had to leave his home and go squat with his friends and relatives as they feared for their lives. This is after the land grabbers camped in his yard yelling that they will take his land and kill his animals if he does not move. Rick is planning to permanently move out of his home of a 100 hectors this weekend as a result. Vati Naaidoo, a member of the same community in Olievenhoutbosch is also terrified of the land grabbers as they camped on his yard the whole weekend.

Peter Sealelo, the man who is taking credit for these invasions, happens to be the local chairperson of the EFF in Olivenhoutbosch. According to him, all they are doing is identifying unused land in their area so that the government can buy it. They will not be erecting any structures, but merely marking the land with tapes and poles. He alleges that Paul Mashitile, the current treasurer general of the ANC told the residents of Olievenhoutbosch in 2017 to do when they identify unused land in their area, he was the chairperson of the ANC at the time. Mr Sealelo says he is not doing this under the EFF banner but merely as a community leader.

Regardless of President Cyril Ramaphosa’s warning against illegal land invasions over the weekend, these dwellers in Olievenhoutbosch seems undeterred and willing to continue wit the invasion. Is this a result of the Land expropriation without compensation that the ANC took as resolution n the elective conference? Are the words of EFF leader Julius Malema encouraging these misdeeds? Have the country’s politician sparked a land uprising that they may not be able to control? Carte Blanche investigates

Press Release:


This past weekend, Pretoria and Johannesburg were marred by illegal land invasion incidents in Olievenhoutbosch, East Lynne and Blue Hills. Rising tensions and misinformation has fueled individuals on the ground, putting people’s homes and safety on the line as private property is invaded.

Script:


RIck: There was hundreds of people here on this property.

Freddie Pienaar: They started throwing stones at the police, then I think the police reacted on that, and someone was hurt

Vassie: I felt very very threatened

Link: There’ve been a series of land grabs in Johannesburg and Pretoria over the past week like here in Olievenhoutbosch, escalating fears of further land invasions.

Rick: They were putting in poles, land poles all over, lints, danger tape marking off places where they want to stay.

VO: Rick Coutsoulis and his family have been tenants for 6 years on a house which is situated on over 100 hectares of zoned farmland in Olievenhoutbosch Centurion. Most of the land lies uncultivated and vacant, with the owner living in Durban. Rick says this is the first time he's felt afraid.

Rick: Then suddenly all of the people were in front of my gate, 10, 20 people maybe - shouting at us , we’re going to take your house, we’re going to kill your animals. We’re going to take this land.

Peter: There is no way whereby any normal person in this country in South Africa can take someone’s property.

VO: Peter Seolela is a community leader in Olievenhoutbosch as well as EFF chairperson for Ward 106 in the area. He says he is merely spearheading a community programme.

Peter: What we are doing here is identifying empty land, and mark them wait for the owners and the government to come together and buy those pieces of land based on the promises of the former MEC of housing Paul Mashatile

VO: Another Olievenhoutbosch resident, Vassie Naidoo owns 9.7 hectares of land, which he also uses for business. He woke up to his fence being torn down.

Vassie: There was hundreds of vehicles driving up and down and they first occupied the property across the road from me. When I went outside and then I see them approaching my property as well and I asked a few people, what are you up to - they said, to acquire the property and they want to put shacks on it.

sound ups and shots of youtube video footage.

VO: These are some of the scenes being shared on social media, in another land invasion on government owned property in East Lynn, Tshwane. Here too people arrived in the early hours of the morning, started erecting shacks and marking land. Freddie Pienaar ward councilor for the DA arrived on the scene.

Freddie: I immediately contacted the land invasion unit, the mayor of Tshwane all were involved, and unfortunately some of the invaders here retaliated.

VO: Several hundred rounds of rubber bullets were fired at the land invaders by the police in order to disperse the crowd

Freddie: Some of the houses were stoned, some of the people had fled the scene and went into the properties of the local residents here and um it was chaos for about two or three hours.

VO: Some people are blaming government's pronouncement to amend the property clause - section 25 of the constitution, for creating fertile ground for land grabs, lawlessness and anarchy.

Sound up Cyril in SONA : We will accelerate out land distribution programme, this approach will include the expropriation of land without compensation.

Ian: I think that what went wrong here is they said things that really inflamed a lot of emotion and they have now caused people to do things like we are seeing here.

VO: Ian Cameron head of Community Safety at Afriforum, has been assisting the community of Olievenhoutbosch and surrounds, to secure their properties and their safety.

Mac: Ian when you say it’s a mixed community, you mean there’s black land owners as well as white landowners.

Ian: Exactly and they all share the same concern that this is not the way to go. The point is just if someone opens a trespassing case, the cops have to act, the police are responsible for making sure that private landowners in the country are also protected

LINK: Families that are living in open pieces of land such as these are feeling more and more intimidated and threatened and are now having to arm themselves because they feel their lives are in danger.

Rick: We are busy packing, I don’t know where we are going to go to yet.. I just don’t know where we are going to go to, but we’re packing, we’re leaving, and it’s heart broken for me. Everybody needs land, everybody needs a place to stay. So let me stay, let me live in peace.

VO: The local neighbourhood watch have come to help protect Rick and his family while he finds somewhere else to live. Vassie Naidoo says the police haven’t been of much assistance.

Vassie: I work hard for the land and I have a bond on it, so you can’t just come and acquire people’s property. I asked a few people what are you up to, they said no the EFF has asked them to mark the land.

Peter: We are saying come and get a piece of land, but it cannot be just come and invade the land

Mac: Peter, how do you control intimidation and violence, we’ve got a farmer just five minutes away from here that is, that has been threatened and it is blamed squarely on your shoulders as the EFF?

Peter: They are supposed to tell us when they see those kind of things, and we’ll come ourselves and deal with those intruders. Another guy down there, there’s an Indian guy, he called me on Sunday and I went there to him, I went straight to him and I showed him that no one can do anything to you, and today if you go there, there’s no one.

VO: Earlier this week, President Cyril Ramaphosa condemned these land grabs:

Cyril Ramaphosa: Where they will go and invade land, and smash and grab land. That will not be allowed, that will be stopped. That is against the tenets of our constitution.

Ian: It’s a massive threat to private landownership in the country. Not only because of the value that decreases, but all the other issues like for example safety.

LINK: It is on vacant properties like this where people have come, demarcated themselves a piece of land just so that they can have a place they call home.

Thulani: Shelter and housing it’s a basic necessity it’s a basic human right

VO: Thulani Nkosi is a Senior Attorney for the Socio Economic Rights Institute:

Thulani: We don’t see all those as land grabs, we see them as land occupations and these land occupations occur because people don’t have shelter

Alpha: If you have a place that you can call your own, you can build on that place. You can turn that place into a home.

VO: Alpha Hadebe, is one of the 25000 residents who were promised land here in Olievenhoutbosch, he says he has been waiting for 24 years for government to deliver on their commitment.

Alpha: I have a son and that son deserves a place that he can call home.

Mac: is this a failure from government to provide housing?
Thulani: Without a doubt. Now if you’ve been waiting for over 2 years for your state to do something for you, for the state to provide housing for you and they haven’t done it, what do you do?


Mac: Politicians have also been blamed for some of the land grabs that have happened, can they take blame for this since this motion was passed in parliament?

Thulani: If you currently look all the latest informal settlements in this country, they have all been as a result of land occupation that was unauthorised.
VO: According to the HLP land audit report of November 2017, currently in South Africa, privately owned land by individuals is: 1,3% black - 1,7% Indian, 4,4% coloured and 22,2% white. The rest of the land totalling 69% , is owned by entities like companies, trusts, SOE’s, Unregistered trust land and the state.
The need for increased black land ownership has reached critical proportions

David Makhura: I want us to give you the land properly.

sound up...

VO: The tensions within the communities rose this week and Gauteng Premier David Makhura attended an urgent community meeting in Olievenhoutbosch.

David: We are dealing with this matter with the land question properly. There is a motion in parliament, we are going to amend the constitution, we are going make sure that our people have land so that they can live meaningful lives. But we won’t allow anarchy and lawlessness.

Ian: What we need to ask for example is to say what is exactly do you mean by land that’s going to be taken, is it any land, is it state land, is it agricultural land, is it urban areas, is it rural areas, cultural land, we need to go through that list. What they’ve described now is exactly the Zimbabwe model.

Thulani: Because we’ve learned lessons in Zimbabwe, that’s the reason not to follow the Zimbabwian situation.

David Makhura: The provincial government and the municipalities in Gauteng are on full alert that we will act across the province. We will act decisively, we will make sure people are arrested, people are prosecuted, for breaking the law.

VO: Despite reassurances from Government some land owners are still afraid they may lose their right to land ownership.

Vassi: I hear that there must be land reform. I agree with that, but I also worked through similiar disadvantages, and I’ve also worked myself to where I am at the moment and I feel if people have to do these sort of things, they have to do it within the law.

Thulani: Remember when the constitution speaks about this issue, it talks about just and equitability You don’t think that you will ever have a situation where you say, I’m not going to pay compensation for all the land just like we say you can’t envisage the situation where I’m going to pay for compensation for every land. It just depends on a case by case situation. But what is key, it’s always this idea that the state and landowners you must negotiate, and through that negotiations a lot of deals could be struck.

VO: Despite reassurances from Government some land owners are still afraid they may lose their right to land ownership. Vassi: I hear that there must be land reform. I agree with that, but I also worked through similiar disadvantages, and I’ve also worked myself to where I am at the moment and I feel if people have to do these sort of things, they have to do it within the law. Thulani: Remember when the constitution speaks about this issue, it talks about just and equitability You don’t think that you will ever have a situation where you say, I’m not going to pay compensation for all the land just like we say you can’t envisage the situation where I’m going to pay for compensation for every land. It just depends on a case by case situation. But what is key, it’s always this idea that the state and landowners you must negotiate, and through that negotiations a lot of deals could be struck.

metadata.Unique Selling Point: In the past few days illegal land occupation took an escalating turn. This follows the ANC and the EFF’s radical stance in parliament on Land expropriation without compensation. Raising tensions and misinformation has fueled aggravated individuals on the ground putting people’s homes and safety on the line as private property is invaded.
metadata.Summary: This past weekend Pretoria was marred by illegal land invasion as incidents in Olievenhoutbosch, East Lynne and the Blue hills caught the headlines. Land grabs in South Africa, particularly in Pretoria, were encouraged about two years ago led by the comments made at the time by EFF leader Julius Malema when he said that people must occupy land where they see it. In Mahube, Mamelodi residents were up in arms after EFF supports erected shacks next to their homes following their leader’s message in 2016. Although Land grabbing is not a new thing in South Africa, it is a strange coincidence that this passed weekend’s incidents come just 2 weeks after parliament’s promise to the masses that the “Land is coming”. On Saturday 10th of March, the Tshwane metro police were forced to use rubber bullets on land invaders. According to Freddie Pienaar, DA ward councilor in East Lynne, the squatters begin erecting shacks along Jan Coetzee and Lanham roads. Freddie believes this was a move that had been planned for sometime although he cannot confirm the instigators. He had to call the Police and Land invasion authorities to come rescue the situation. At the same time in Mnandi, Olievenhoutbosch, residents were also shocked to see people in their privately owned properties marking spaces with poles and saying it now their land. An initiative led by a certain Peter Sealelo, a community leader in Olievenhoutbosch, members of the community have went out to camp on privately owned land claiming that it is unused land that they are now claiming for themselves. A similar case of land grabbing occurred in Blue Hills.
metadata.Further information: Residents in Olievenhoutbosch were threatened and some had to vacate their homes. Rick, one of the resident, says he and his family had to leave his home and go squat with his friends and relatives as they feared for their lives. This is after the land grabbers camped in his yard yelling that they will take his land and kill his animals if he does not move. Rick is planning to permanently move out of his home of a 100 hectors this weekend as a result. Vati Naaidoo, a member of the same community in Olievenhoutbosch is also terrified of the land grabbers as they camped on his yard the whole weekend. Peter Sealelo, the man who is taking credit for these invasions, happens to be the local chairperson of the EFF in Olivenhoutbosch. According to him, all they are doing is identifying unused land in their area so that the government can buy it. They will not be erecting any structures, but merely marking the land with tapes and poles. He alleges that Paul Mashitile, the current treasurer general of the ANC told the residents of Olievenhoutbosch in 2017 to do when they identify unused land in their area, he was the chairperson of the ANC at the time. Mr Sealelo says he is not doing this under the EFF banner but merely as a community leader. Regardless of President Cyril Ramaphosa’s warning against illegal land invasions over the weekend, these dwellers in Olievenhoutbosch seems undeterred and willing to continue wit the invasion. Is this a result of the Land expropriation without compensation that the ANC took as resolution n the elective conference? Are the words of EFF leader Julius Malema encouraging these misdeeds? Have the country’s politician sparked a land uprising that they may not be able to control? Carte Blanche investigates
